title: Stubborn Channa
hookLine: the old charioteer is hard to admonish; the Buddha's last instruction is that the community leave him to himself, and the silence turns him (DN 16; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)

lines: THE CHARIOTEER WHO RODE OUT WITH HIM.
A MONK WHO WON'T BE TOLD.
cards: Back in year one, on the night the prince left the palace, one man was awake with him: Channa, his charioteer, who saddled the horse Kanthaka and rode out beside him.
Years later Channa becomes a monk, and that's where the trouble starts. The commentaries say he couldn't forget whose friend he'd been first.

It was our Buddha, our teaching, he'd say, and he brushed off the elders who tried to correct him. Then the Buddha is dying, and among the last things he tells Ananda is what should be done about Channa.

teach.h: THE HIGHER PENALTY: LET HIM BE.
teach.b: First, the instruction. In the Mahaparinibbana discourse, the Buddha tells Ananda that after he has gone, Channa should receive the higher penalty, the brahmadanda. What is it, Ananda asks.

Let Channa say whatever he likes, the Buddha says, but the monks should neither speak to him, nor advise him, nor instruct him. No expulsion, no scolding: the people he kept brushing off will simply stop trying.
Second, the news. The Vinaya tells what happened after the council. Ananda travels to Kosambi, where Channa is living, and tells him.
And Channa, hearing that the community will no longer speak to him, falls down in a faint. The proud man, it turns out, cared very much. Third, the turn.
Troubled and ashamed, the text says, he goes off to live alone, earnest, diligent, resolute, and before long he reaches the goal the whole path points to.
The man who wouldn't accept a word of advice finds the way himself, once nobody is pushing. Fourth, the lifting.

Channa asks Ananda to lift the penalty, and Ananda answers that it was lifted already, the moment he was freed. The silence was never meant to outlast the stubbornness; it was the space he needed to soften.
The story doesn't make Channa a villain. It makes him the proof: if the charioteer who argued with everyone can wake up, the story suggests, no stubbornness is out of reach.
That closes our days with Upali, Anuruddha, Rahula and Channa.

how: Theravada teachers tell Channa's story as an example of how a community's restraint, rather than punishment, can leave room for a proud person to change, and of how hard it can be to accept advice.

o: the monk who tried to split the order
the horse that carried the prince away
the charioteer-monk who wouldn't be told

p: nobody speaks to, advises or instructs him
lifted the moment he was freed

s: the higher penalty expelled Channa from the order
he stayed a monk; the community simply stopped speaking to, advising or instructing him.
Channa fainted when he heard the news
the Vinaya says he fell down in a faint, then went off alone, ashamed, and practiced hard.
the Vinaya says he reached the goal, and Ananda told him the penalty ended at that moment.

games.q: you're Ananda. Channa, now freed, asks you to lift the penalty. what do you say?
o: "I'll ask the elders to vote on it."
"it was lifted the moment you were freed."
"you'll have to wait a while longer."
games.why: Ananda tells him the penalty was lifted already, at the moment he was freed. the silence had done its work.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you dig in: an argument you always have the same way, a piece of advice you keep refusing, a habit someone has named more than once.

Don't argue with it, and don't give in yet; just set it down in front of you, the way the community finally left Channa alone with himself. Breathe beside it, and notice whether it feels as hard as it did a minute ago.

wordCard.voice: Stubborn Channa. The old charioteer who wouldn't be told, left to himself, and freed. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali brahmadanda: the 'higher penalty' given to Channa, the community's silence toward him.

carryVoice: Your line: even Channa. Sometimes a little silence does what advice couldn't. Day seven hundred fifty-two.
